explanation.form-i-pattern.a-a: Past fatḥa ({pastForm}), present fatḥa ({presentForm}). Roots with ح، ع، غ، خ as a middle or final radical often follow this pattern, but there are many exceptions.
explanation.form-i-pattern.a-i: Past fatḥa ({pastForm}), present kasra ({presentForm}). Learn the vowels together with the verb.
explanation.form-i-pattern.a-u: Past fatḥa ({pastForm}), present ḍamma ({presentForm}). Learn the vowels together with the verb.
explanation.form-i-pattern.i-a: Past kasra ({pastForm}), present fatḥa ({presentForm}). Learn the vowels together with the verb.
explanation.form-i-pattern.i-i: Past kasra ({pastForm}), present kasra ({presentForm}). A small class, mostly roots with a weak first radical.
explanation.form-i-pattern.i-u: Past kasra ({pastForm}), present ḍamma ({presentForm}). Extremely rare, if it happens at all.
explanation.form-i-pattern.u-a: Past ḍamma ({pastForm}), present fatḥa ({presentForm}). Extremely rare, if it happens at all.
explanation.form-i-pattern.u-i: Past ḍamma ({pastForm}), present kasra ({presentForm}). Extremely rare, if it happens at all.
explanation.form-i-pattern.u-u: Past ḍamma ({pastForm}), present ḍamma ({presentForm}). Learn the vowels together with the verb.
explanation.form-root.assimilation-compl: In Form VIII, a first radical of د، ذ، ث، ط or ظ swallows the تَ completely: a doubled letter appears where the تَ would be.
explanation.form-root.assimilation-empha: In Form VIII, a first radical of ص or ض turns the تَ into the emphatic طَ.
explanation.form-root.assimilation-hamza: In Form VIII, a first-radical hamza merges into the تَ and doubles it; the hamza itself disappears.
explanation.form-root.assimilation-voici: In Form VIII, a first radical of ز turns the تَ into the voiced دَ.
explanation.form-root.assimilation-weak-: A weak first radical merges into the Form VIII ت and doubles it.
explanation.form.1-action: A fatḥa in the past usually means an action done to something, or out in the world. It is the widest Form I group.
explanation.form.1-intermediate: A kasra in the past usually means thinking or feeling: halfway between an action and a state.
explanation.form.1-stative: A ḍamma in the past usually means a quality the subject simply has, so the imperative is rarely meaningful here.
explanation.form.10: The اِسْتَـ prefix (اِسْتَفْعَلَ) marks Form X. It usually means to seek, request, or consider the Form I action.
explanation.form.2: The doubled middle radical marks Form II. It usually adds force, or makes the verb cause something.
explanation.form.3: The long vowel after the first radical (فَاعَلَ) marks Form III. It usually means acting with or towards someone else.
explanation.form.4: The hamza at the front (أَفْعَلَ) marks Form IV. It usually makes the verb cause something, or declare it to be so.
explanation.form.5: The ت prefix with a doubled middle radical (تَفَعَّلَ) marks Form V. It usually turns the action back on the doer, or means entering a state.
explanation.form.6: The ت prefix with a long vowel after the first radical (تَفَاعَلَ) marks Form VI. It usually means acting on one another.
explanation.form.7: The اِنْ prefix (اِنْفَعَلَ) marks Form VII. It usually turns the Form I action into entering a state, or into something done to the subject.
explanation.form.8: The ت slipped in after the first radical (اِفْتَعَلَ) marks Form VIII. It usually turns the action inward, back on the doer.
explanation.form.8-wasl: The اِ at the front is hamzat al-wasl: it carries the opening cluster when the verb stands alone, and drops after a word ending in a vowel.
explanation.form.9: The alif at the front with a doubled last radical (اِفْعَلَّ) marks Form IX, used for colors and bodily defects.
explanation.form.1q: Four-letter roots follow فَعْلَلَ (Form Iq). All four radicals together carry the core meaning.
explanation.form.2q: The تَ prefix on Form Iq (تَفَعْلَلَ) marks Form IIq: for four-letter roots it usually turns the action back on the doer, or means entering a state.
explanation.form.3q: The اِ prefix with نـ between the second and third radicals (اِفْعَنْلَلَ) marks Form IIIq: the action turns back on the doer or is done to it. Form IIIq is rare.
explanation.form.4q: The اِ prefix with the last two radicals doubled (اِفْعَلَلَّ) marks Form IVq, used for colors and physical states. Form IVq is very rare.
explanation.nominal-root.geminate-contra: The pattern leaves no vowel between the identical radicals, so they merge into one doubled letter (شَدَّة): {arabic}.
explanation.nominal-root.geminate-separa: The pattern puts a vowel between the identical radicals, so both stay written out: {arabic}.
explanation.nominal-root.hollow-hamza: In Form I the weak middle radical surfaces as a hamza in the active participle: {arabic}.
explanation.nominal-root.hollow-long-vow: In Form I the weak middle radical stays as the pattern's own long vowel in the passive participle: {arabic}.
explanation.nominal-root.hollow-voice-se: The weak middle radical is spelled ي in the active participle and ا in the passive: {arabic}.
explanation.nominal-root.hollow-always-a: The weak middle radical is always spelled ا here, in both the active and the passive participle: {arabic}.
explanation.nominal-root.defective-form-: In Form I the weak last radical drops out of the active participle, leaving a bare ending: {arabic}.
In Form I the weak last radical doubles into the passive participle's ending instead: {arabic}.
explanation.nominal-root.defective-tanwe: The weak last radical folds into the active participle's ending: {arabic}.
The weak last radical folds into the passive participle's ending, spelled with a final ى: {arabic}.
explanation.nominal.activeParticiple: The active participle (اسم الفاعل) names the one doing the action: Forms II–X take a مُـ prefix, and Form I follows فَاعِل.
explanation.nominal.activeParticiple.for: This verb’s Form I active participle is lexical, not the regular فَاعِل pattern. Memorize it alongside the verb.

A common Form I lexical pattern is فَعِيل, an adjective for a fixed attribute, especially a quality seen as part of someone’s nature. It usually follows the meaning of the verb, but you should still memorize it.
explanation.nominal.activeParticiple.qua: The active participle (اسم الفاعل) of a four-letter verb always takes a مُـ prefix. In Form Iq the pattern is مُفَعْلِل.
explanation.nominal.masdar.form-i: In Form I, the masdar is lexical: memorize it alongside the verb. Common patterns as anchors: فَعْل (momentary action), فُعُول (motion), فِعَالَة (craft), but these are tendencies, not rules.
explanation.nominal.masdar.form-i-mimi: This Form I mīmī masdar follows the pattern {pattern}. A mīmī masdar starts with مـ and names the action; because it can look like a noun of time or place, use context to confirm it is a masdar here.
explanation.nominal.masdar.1q: Apply the regular فَعْلَلَة pattern to get the Form Iq masdar: no separate memorization needed, unlike the triliteral Form I masdar.
explanation.nominal.masdar.2q: Apply the تَفَعْلُل pattern to get the Form IIq masdar: the action noun for the reflexive or inchoative quadriliteral.
explanation.nominal.masdar.3q: Apply the اِفْعِنْلَال pattern to get the Form IIIq masdar: reflexive or passive action of a transitive quadriliteral. Form IIIq is rare.
explanation.nominal.masdar.4q: Apply the اِفْعِلَّال pattern to get the Form IVq masdar: colors or physical states. Form IVq is very rare.
explanation.nominal.masdar.non-form-i: The Form {form} masdar applies the pattern {pattern} to the root.
explanation.nominal.passiveParticiple: The passive participle (اسم المفعول) names the one the action is done to: Forms II–X take a مُـ prefix, and Form I follows مَفْعُول.
explanation.nominal.passiveParticiple.qu: The passive participle (اسم المفعول) of a four-letter verb always takes a مُـ prefix. In Form Iq the pattern is مُفَعْلَل.
explanation.pronoun.assimilated-nun: The ending’s own ن merges with the verb’s final ن, so the two are written as a single نّ.
explanation.pronoun.base-form: For {pronounLabel} nothing is added: {arabic} is the verb unchanged.
explanation.pronoun.dropped-prefix: In this form, drop the prefix {elidedPrefix}.
explanation.pronoun.dropped-suffix: The jussive and subjunctive drop the nūn ending {elidedSuffix} that the indicative would have.
explanation.pronoun.prefix-and-suffix: To conjugate for {pronounLabel}: attach {prefix} at the front and {suffix} at the end → {arabic}.
explanation.pronoun.prefix-only: To conjugate for {pronounLabel}: attach {prefix} at the front → {arabic}.
explanation.pronoun.suffix-only: To conjugate for {pronounLabel}: attach {suffix} at the end → {arabic}.
explanation.root.assimilated: The first radical {initialRadical} is weak. A و usually drops in the Form I present and imperative before a fatḥa or kasra, leaving what looks like a two-letter root; it stays before a ḍamma and in some verbs with a kasra in the past, and a ي always stays.
explanation.root.assimilated-sound-form: Outside Form I the first letter {initialRadical} is stable: it stays in the verb instead of dropping.
explanation.root.defective-waw: Watch the last radical و: with no ending it becomes a long vowel, before a personal ending it comes back as a consonant, and in the jussive and imperative it drops.
explanation.root.defective-yaa: Watch the last radical ي: with no ending it becomes a long vowel, before a personal ending it comes back as a consonant, and in the jussive and imperative it drops.
explanation.root.doubled: The second and third radicals are the same in {root}.
explanation.root.assimilated-defective-w: Two of the radicals are weak: the first, {initialRadical}, and a final و. Expect both the assimilated and the defective pattern.
explanation.root.assimilated-defective-y: Two of the radicals are weak: the first, {initialRadical}, and a final ي. Expect both the assimilated and the defective pattern.
explanation.root.assimilated-hollow-waw: Two of the radicals are weak: the first, {initialRadical}, and a middle و. Expect both the assimilated and the hollow pattern.
explanation.root.assimilated-hollow-yaa: Two of the radicals are weak: the first, {initialRadical}, and a middle ي. Expect both the assimilated and the hollow pattern.
explanation.root.hamzated-defective-waw: One radical is hamza and the last radical is و: both are irregular, so follow each one separately.
explanation.root.hamzated-defective-yaa: One radical is hamza and the last radical is ي: both are irregular, so follow each one separately.
explanation.root.hamzated-doubled: One radical is hamza, and the second and third radicals are the same: expect the hamza to change spelling and the pair to merge.
explanation.root.hamzated-hollow-defecti: Three irregularities combine: a hamza at the front, a weak middle radical, and a weak last radical. Each one needs separate attention.
explanation.root.hamzated-hollow-waw: One radical is hamza and the middle radical is و: expect both hamza spelling changes and hollow verb behavior.
explanation.root.hamzated-hollow-yaa: One radical is hamza and the middle radical is ي: expect both hamza spelling changes and hollow verb behavior.
explanation.root.hamzated: One radical is hamza (ء): its written shape changes with the vowels around it, so check the spelling in each form.
explanation.root.hollow-defective-waw: Two of the radicals are weak: the middle و and the last one. The last one leads, so this verb follows the defective pattern.
explanation.root.hollow-defective-yaa: Two of the radicals are weak: the middle ي and the last one. The last one leads, so this verb follows the defective pattern.
explanation.root.hollow-waw: Watch the middle radical و: it becomes a long vowel, but shortens before an ending that starts with a consonant, so the verb looks different in the past and the present.
explanation.root.hollow-yaa: Watch the middle radical ي: it becomes a long vowel, but shortens before an ending that starts with a consonant, so the verb looks different in the past and the present.
explanation.root.doubled-sound-form: Forms II and V already double the middle radical, so the identical pair in this root never merges: both stay written out.
explanation.root.hollow-sound-form: In Forms II, III, V, VI and IX the weak middle radical stays an ordinary consonant: the doubling or the long vowel of the pattern protects it, so this verb behaves like a sound verb throughout.
explanation.root.hollow-uncontracted-waw: The middle radical و looks like a hollow root, but this verb never lengthens it to a long vowel: it behaves like a sound verb throughout.
explanation.root.hollow-uncontracted-yaa: The middle radical ي looks like a hollow root, but this verb never lengthens it to a long vowel: it behaves like a sound verb throughout.
explanation.root.sound: Every radical in {root} is stable: apply the pattern directly, with no irregular changes.
explanation.tense-root.final-drops: In the jussive and imperative, forms with no ending drop the last weak letter completely: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-elides: In the active past, the third-person feminine singular and dual drop the last weak letter silently, and the middle radical takes a short fatḥa: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-isolated: In the third-person masculine singular active past, the last weak letter drops and a long ā ending is left: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-lengthens-i: With no ending, the last radical is written as a long ī: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-lengthens-u: With no ending, the last radical is written as a long ū: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-passive-aa: With no ending, the passive present of a verb with a weak last radical ends in ـَى: the last radical becomes ā whether the root ends in و or ي. Result: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-passive-ya: In the passive past, the last weak letter appears as ي after the kasra, whether the root ends in و or ي: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-passive-uu: In the passive past, the masculine plural ending absorbs the last weak letter into a long ū: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-resurfaces: In the active past, before plural and personal endings, the last weak letter always comes back as a consonant: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.final-surfaces-co: Here the last weak letter is not a long vowel: it appears as a consonant, or merges into the ending’s own vowel. Result: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.geminate-contract: No consonant separates them here, so the identical radicals of {root} merge into one doubled letter: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.geminate-jussive: In the jussive and imperative more than one form is correct: the merged {arabic}, the same form ending in kasra instead of fatḥa, and a written-out form that keeps the identical radicals apart with a sukūn between them.
explanation.tense-root.geminate-separate: Before an ending that starts with a consonant, the identical radicals stay apart and the verb shows both: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.hamza-madda: Two hamzas meeting at the start merge into alif madda. Result: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.hamza-elides: The initial hamza drops here instead of taking a seat, leaving {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.hamza-seat: As a tendency, the hamza takes the seat matching the stronger of its own vowel and the one before it: kasra → ي, ḍamma → و, fatḥa → ا. It tends to be written bare as ء after a long vowel, and where neither side offers a vowel. The spelling has more cases than one rule covers, so read the form itself: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.initial-retained: The present vowel is ḍamma, so the initial و stays: the result is {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.initial-retained-: This verb keeps the initial و even before a fatḥa, as many verbs with a kasra in the past do: the result is {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.initial-drops: The Form I active present drops the initial و: the result is {arabic}. It comes back in every other form.
explanation.tense-root.middle-lengthens-: In the active past, the weak middle radical becomes a long ā: {arabic}. Roots with و and with ي both use this vowel.
explanation.tense-root.middle-shortens-c: An ending that starts with a consonant forces the weak middle radical to shorten: {arabic}. Roots with و and with ي both lose the long vowel here.
explanation.tense-root.middle-lengthens-: In the active present, the weak middle radical is written as a long ī: {arabic}.
In the active present, the weak middle radical is written as a long ū: {arabic}.
In the active present of Forms IV and X, the weak middle radical is always a long ī, whatever the radical: {arabic}.
In the active present, the weak middle radical is a long ā here, whatever the radical: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.middle-passive-aa: In the passive present, the weak middle radical becomes a long ā for roots with و and with ي alike: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.middle-passive-ii: In the passive past, the weak middle radical becomes a long ī for roots with و and with ي alike: {arabic}.
explanation.tense-root.middle-shortens: In the jussive and imperative, the weak middle radical always shortens and the last radical takes sukūn: {arabic}.
explanation.tense.active.future: For the future, add سَـ or سَوْفَ to the present indicative. Nothing else changes.
explanation.tense.active.imperative.elis: For the imperative, start from the jussive and drop the second-person prefix.
explanation.tense.active.imperative.supp: If that leaves two consonants colliding, add alif al-wasl (ا) at the front.
explanation.tense.active.past.form-i: The third-person masculine singular {pastForm} is the form this verb is listed under: no prefix, and {pastVowel} on the second radical.
explanation.tense.active.past: Use the active past for completed actions.
explanation.tense.active.present.indicat: Use the active present indicative for actions that are ongoing or habitual.
explanation.tense.active.present.jussive: After لَمْ and in conditionals, use the jussive instead of the indicative. Build it from the present indicative.
explanation.tense.active.present.subjunc: After أَنْ, لَنْ and similar particles, use the subjunctive instead of the indicative. Build it from the present indicative.
explanation.tense.passive.future: For the passive future, add سَـ or سَوْفَ to the passive present indicative.
explanation.tense.passive.present.indica: Use the passive present for actions that are ongoing or habitual.
explanation.tense.passive.present.jussiv: After لَمْ and in conditionals, use the passive jussive.
explanation.tense.passive.present.subjun: After أَنْ, لَنْ and similar particles, use the passive subjunctive.
explanation.voice.passive.future: Like every passive built on the present: ḍamma on the prefix, fatḥa before the last consonant.
explanation.voice.passive.past: You can spot the passive past by the ḍamma on the first syllable, and usually by a kasra before the last consonant - a contracted doubled letter swallows it.
explanation.voice.passive.present.indica: You can spot the passive present by the ḍamma on the prefix and the fatḥa before the last consonant.
explanation.voice.passive.present.jussiv: You can spot the passive present by the ḍamma on the prefix and the fatḥa before the last consonant.
explanation.voice.passive.present.subjun: You can spot the passive present by the ḍamma on the prefix and the fatḥa before the last consonant.

formInfo.form1.relationship: Other patterns reshape this base meaning (causative, reflexive, mutual, stative).
formInfo.form10.relationship: It extends Form I or IV; many roots also appear in Form II for a direct causative.
formInfo.form2.relationship: Form II adds someone who makes the action happen to another. Form V turns that back on the doer.
formInfo.form3.relationship: The other party is not acted on but acts too: the action runs between two equals and usually keeps going. Form VI makes that mutual sense explicit.
formInfo.form4.relationship: Form X often expresses seeking or considering that causative meaning.
formInfo.form5.relationship: The doer causes the change and undergoes it, bringing the state about in itself. That covers both gradually becoming something and pretending to be it.
formInfo.form6.relationship: Form VI spells out the shared action of Form III: each side acts on the other at the same time.
formInfo.form7.relationship: Think “to become” or “to be acted upon” compared with the plain Form I verb.
formInfo.form8.relationship: Compare with Form I; some roots also use Form VII when the sense is more passive.
formInfo.form9.relationship: They rarely pair with other forms but still anchor to the base Form I meaning.

rootInfo.assimilated.description: This is an assimilated root (initial weak), where the first radical is a glide (و or ي). The initial glide typically disappears in the Form I imperfect and imperative, making the verb appear biliteral in those cells.
rootInfo.biliteral.description: This is a biliteral root, quadriliteral by reduplication: the first two radicals repeat as the third and fourth. The repetition is a mark of the root itself and often signals intensive, repeated, or onomatopoeic action.
rootInfo.defective-waw.description: This is a defective root with a wāw (و) as the third radical. It surfaces as a long vowel in the imperfect but drops before consonant-initial suffixes.
rootInfo.defective-yaa.description: This is a defective root with a yāʾ (ي) as the third radical. It surfaces as a long vowel in the imperfect but drops before consonant-initial suffixes, shortening the preceding vowel.
rootInfo.defective.description: This is a defective root (final weak), where the third radical is a glide (و or ي). It surfaces as a long vowel in the imperfect but deletes before consonant-initial suffixes, causing the preceding vowel to shorten.
rootInfo.doubled.description: This is a doubled root, where the second and third radicals are identical. They merge into a single geminated consonant (šadda) when no vowel separates them, but split apart before consonant-initial suffixes with a short vowel inserted between them.
rootInfo.assimilated-defective-waw.descr: This is a doubly weak root with two weak radicals, where the dominant weak behavior is waw-like (و).
rootInfo.assimilated-defective-yaa.descr: This is a doubly weak root with two weak radicals, where the dominant weak behavior is yaa-like (ي).
rootInfo.assimilated-hollow-waw.descript: This is a doubly weak root with two weak radicals, where the dominant weak behavior is waw-like (و).
rootInfo.assimilated-hollow-yaa.descript: This is a doubly weak root with two weak radicals, where the dominant weak behavior is yaa-like (ي).
rootInfo.hamzated-defective-waw.descript: This root combines a hamza (ء) with a defective final radical that is specifically و.
rootInfo.hamzated-defective-yaa.descript: This root combines a hamza (ء) with a defective final radical that is specifically ي.
rootInfo.hamzated-defective.description: This root combines a hamza (ء) with a defective pattern (final weak). The initial radical is a hamza and the final radical is weak (و, ي, or ا).
rootInfo.hamzated-doubled.description: This root combines a hamza (ء) with a doubled pattern. It contains a hamza and has identical second and third radicals, which often surface as a geminated consonant.
rootInfo.hamzated-hollow-defective.descr: This root combines multiple irregularities: it contains a hamza (ء) at the initial position, has a weak middle radical (و or ي), and has a weak final radical (و, ي, or ا). This combination requires special handling in conjugation.
rootInfo.hamzated-hollow-waw.description: This root combines a hamza (ء) with a hollow middle radical that is specifically و.
rootInfo.hamzated-hollow-yaa.description: This root combines a hamza (ء) with a hollow middle radical that is specifically ي.
rootInfo.hamzated-hollow.description: This root combines a hamza (ء) with a hollow pattern (middle weak). The initial radical is a hamza and the middle radical is weak (و or ي).
rootInfo.hamzated.description: This root contains a hamza (ء) as one of its three radicals. It conjugates like a strong root, but the written form of ء changes depending on the surrounding vowel environment (its “seat”).
rootInfo.hollow-defective-waw.descriptio: This is a doubly weak root with two weak radicals, where the dominant weak behavior is waw-like (و).
rootInfo.hollow-defective-yaa.descriptio: This is a doubly weak root with two weak radicals, where the dominant weak behavior is yaa-like (ي).
rootInfo.hollow-waw.description: This is a hollow root with a wāw (و) glide as the second radical. It surfaces as long /ā/ in the imperfect and imperative; in perfective suffix-initial cells, the glide drops and the vowel shortens.
rootInfo.hollow-yaa.description: This is a hollow root with a yāʾ (ي) glide as the second radical. It surfaces as long /ī/ in the imperfect and imperative; in perfective suffix-initial cells, the glide drops and the vowel shortens.
rootInfo.hollow.description: This is a hollow root (middle weak), where the second radical is a glide (و or ي). The glide surfaces as a long vowel (ā or ī) in the imperfect and imperative, making the perfect and imperfect stems look very different.
rootInfo.sound.description: This is a strong root with all radicals being consonants. Strong roots form the foundation of Arabic verb morphology and can appear in all ten verb forms.

explanation.root.biliteral: The four radicals are the first two repeated: {root} is reduplicated, not doubled, so each copy stays a plain consonant and the quadriliteral pattern applies unchanged.
explanation.tense-root.final-lengthens-a: With no ending, the last radical becomes ā and the present closes on ـَى: {arabic}.
explanation.root.hamzated-assimilated: A weak first radical and a hamza: the verb changes between past and present, and the hamza changes its written shape with the vowels around it.
rootInfo.hamzated-assimilated.descriptio: A root with a weak first radical and a hamza. The first radical drops in the Form I present and imperative, while the hamza changes its written seat with the surrounding vowels.
explanation.root.hamzated-assimilated-de: Three irregularities combine: a weak first radical, a hamza, and a last radical ي. Each one needs separate attention.
rootInfo.hamzated-assimilated-defective-: A root combining a weak first radical, a hamza and a final yāʾ. All three behave irregularly, so each has to be tracked separately.
explanation.root.assimilated-doubled: A weak first radical, and identical second and third letters: the verb changes between past and present, and the pair merges into one doubled letter.
rootInfo.assimilated-doubled.description: A root with a weak first radical whose second and third radicals are identical. The identical pair contracts into a geminate when no vowel separates them, and that contracted stem keeps the first radical in the Form I present (وَدَّ، يَوَدُّ).
explanation.laysa.frozen: لَيْسَ is a frozen verb (فِعْل جامِد): these past-tense forms are all it has, with no present, imperative, participle or masdar, so no Form I vowel class applies to it.
explanation.laysa.meaning: The form is past but the meaning is present: لَيْسَ negates a nominal sentence. Like كَانَ it takes a nominative subject and an accusative predicate.
explanation.laysa.radical: Its middle ي is a plain consonant, not a hollow root’s long vowel: it carries sukūn in لَيْسَ and drops altogether before a consonant-initial ending (لَسْتُ, لَسْنَا).
